notes.h: Buying fresh, frozen, canned, dried and pre-prepared produce
points: Fresh: choose firm produce with no bruising, cuts or discolouration; in-season produce is usually cheaper and has the best flavour.
Frozen: picked and frozen soon after harvest, frozen fruit and vegetables retain most of their nutrients, and the product can be cooked from frozen.
Canned: cooked and sealed in tins or jars; canned fruit is usually packed in syrup or juice, and canned vegetables often contain added salt.
Dried: most of the water is removed, so dried fruit such as raisins and apricots keeps for long periods but is concentrated in sugar and energy.
Pre-prepared: washed, peeled, cut or ready-to-cook products such as salad bags and vegetable stir-fry mixes; these are convenient but cost more and have a shorter shelf life than whole produce.

notes.b: Fresh fruit and vegetables are graded under EU marketing standards by the condition of the produce.
points: Extra class: the best quality, uniform in shape, size and colour, and free from defects.
Class I: good quality, with minor defects allowed provided they do not affect general appearance, keeping quality or presentation.
Class II: acceptable quality with more defects allowed, but still fit for consumption.
Indicators of quality include firmness, colour, freshness, absence of bruising and uniform size.
The Bord Bia quality mark on Irish produce indicates that it has met quality assurance standards.
EU food information rules, Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, require the country of origin to be given for fresh fruit and vegetables.

notes.h: Effects of storage and storage guidelines
points: Fresh vegetables should be refrigerated at about 5 degrees Celsius or below and used as soon as possible, because vitamin C declines during storage.
Salad vegetables keep best in a bag in the refrigerator, which limits moisture loss without trapping condensation.
Potatoes should be stored in a cool, dark, dry, ventilated place; light makes them turn green and develop bitter, potentially harmful solanine.
Onions and root vegetables keep best in a cool, dry, ventilated place; damp conditions encourage rot.
Apples release ethylene, a gas that speeds the ripening of other produce, so they should be stored apart from vegetables.
Bananas and other tropical fruit are ripened at room temperature and refrigerated only once ripe.
Frozen fruit and vegetables are stored at minus 18 degrees Celsius or below.
Canned food is kept in a cool, dry place, and dented, swollen or leaking cans are discarded.
Fresh produce is stored away from raw meat to prevent cross-contamination.
Enzymes remain active after harvesting; they continue the ripening process until the produce becomes over-ripe, soft and eventually decays.
When cells are cut or bruised, oxidase is released and reacts with oxygen, causing enzymic browning.
Enzymic browning also destroys some vitamin C and carotene.
Blanching before freezing denatures the enzymes; unblanched vegetables continue to deteriorate even in a freezer.
Moisture is lost through respiration and evaporation, especially in warm, dry, uncovered storage.
Loss of water causes cells to lose turgor: leafy vegetables wilt, roots shrivel and skins wrinkle.
Produce loses mass and becomes limp, with poorer texture and appearance.
Humid refrigerated storage and suitable packaging slow moisture loss.
Bacteria, yeasts and moulds come from soil, dirty hands, equipment, pests, damaged produce and cross-contamination.
Bruises and cuts give micro-organisms access to nutrients and moisture.
Warmth, time and a suitable pH allow micro-organisms to multiply rapidly.
Bacteria cause soft, slimy rot and unpleasant odours; moulds form coloured fuzzy growth and some produce harmful mycotoxins.
Prevention: good hygiene, removing damaged items, separating produce from raw meat, refrigeration and prompt use.
Food businesses must follow the hygiene rules in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, given effect in Ireland by the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland, established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, gives food safety guidance on handling and storing produce.

keyTerms.definition: The brown discolouration of cut or bruised produce caused by oxidase reacting with oxygen.
Brief immersion of vegetables in boiling water, followed by rapid cooling, before freezing.
The pressure of water inside plant cells that keeps leaves and stems firm; loss of turgor causes wilting.
A toxic substance produced by some moulds growing on food.
The highest EU marketing grade for fresh fruit and vegetables, uniform and free from defects.
A gas given off by ripening fruit such as apples, which speeds the ripening of nearby produce.
The transfer of micro-organisms from raw food, surfaces or hands to food that will not be cooked.
The continued breakdown of stored sugars in harvested produce, which releases water and heat.

factCards.term: Three causes of spoilage in vegetables
factCards.definition: Enzymes, moisture loss and microbial contamination.

factCards.term: Storage temperature for frozen fruit and vegetables
Three EU marketing grades for fresh produce
factCards.definition: Extra, Class I and Class II.

factCards.term: Two effects of long storage on fresh vegetables
factCards.definition: Vitamin C is lost, and texture and appearance deteriorate.

factCards.term: Why blanching is done before freezing
factCards.definition: It denatures enzymes that would otherwise cause deterioration during freezer storage.

factCards.term: Produce that should be kept apart from apples
factCards.definition: Vegetables, because apples release ethylene, which speeds up their ripening.

factCards.term: Main nutritional drawback of dried fruit
factCards.definition: It is concentrated in sugar and energy because most of its water has been removed.

factCards.term: Hazard that causes mould growth on stored vegetables
factCards.definition: Mycotoxins are produced by some moulds, and bruised or damaged produce allows moulds to grow.

questions.prompt: Outline two reasons why fresh vegetables lose quality during storage.
questions.model: Any two: vitamin C declines with time in storage; moisture is lost by respiration and evaporation, so vegetables wilt and lose texture; enzymes continue ripening and softening until the produce decays; micro-organisms multiply, especially where produce is damaged or stored warm.

questions.prompt: Describe how enzymes, moisture loss and micro-organisms each reduce the quality of stored fresh vegetables, and explain the storage and handling measures that prevent each cause.
questions.model: Enzymes: continue ripening after harvest, softening the produce until it decays; oxidase released from cut or bruised cells causes enzymic browning and destroys some vitamin C; prevention is prompt use, refrigeration and blanching before freezing. Moisture loss: respiration and evaporation lower cell turgor, so leafy vegetables wilt, roots shrivel and produce loses mass and texture; prevention is humid refrigerated storage, suitable packaging that does not trap condensation and avoiding warm, dry, uncovered storage. Micro-organisms: bacteria, yeasts and moulds enter from soil, hands, equipment, pests and damaged produce; bruises give access to nutrients and moisture; warmth and time allow rapid growth; bacteria cause soft slimy rot and moulds cause coloured fuzzy growth and mycotoxins; prevention is hygiene, removing damaged items, separating produce from raw meat, refrigeration at about 5 degrees Celsius or below and prompt use.
